title: Reconstruction of a complete group from its discrete orbit functor
statement:
Let $G$ be a Hausdorff topological group whose identity has a basis of open subgroups. Assume that $G$ is compact, or complete for the two-sided uniformity: every net Cauchy for both $g_i^{-1}g_j$ and $g_ig_j^{-1}$ converges. Let $\mathcal O_G$ be the small category [def-nagata-category] with objects the left $G$-sets $G/U$ for open subgroups $U\subseteq G$, and with all $G$-equivariant maps as arrows. Give these sets the discrete topology. Write $\omega_G:\mathcal O_G\to\mathbf{Set}$ for the underlying-set functor. Topologize $\operatorname{Aut}(\omega_G)$ by pointwise convergence on all its underlying sets: basic identity neighborhoods fix finitely many specified elements of finitely many $G/U$. Then the map
$$G\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(\omega_G),\qquad g\longmapsto(s\longmapsto gs)_{G/U}$$
is an isomorphism of topological groups. Equivalently one obtains the same automorphism group and topology using the forgetful functor on all discrete continuous left $G$-sets; restriction to $\mathcal O_G$ induces this identification. Categories and sets are placed in compatible universes.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5, pp. 63–64, with Example 7.1.6 for the compact case; orbit-category formulation from the proof (the objects G/U determine a natural automorphism on all disjoint unions).

proof.text: Use [def-nagata-category] for the category axioms: identities and composites of equivariant maps are equivariant. The open subgroups form a set, and each arrow set is a subset of the functions between two quotient sets, so $\mathcal O_G$ is small in the stipulated universes. The underlying-set functor simply keeps these maps. A natural automorphism $\alpha$ is a family of bijections $\alpha_U:G/U\to G/U$ satisfying $f\alpha_U=\alpha_Vf$ for every equivariant arrow $f:G/U\to G/V$. Its inverse family satisfies the same identities.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5, printed p. 64; elementary orbit-coordinate expansion of its coset-filter argument.

proof.text: For $g\in G$, left translation on every $G/U$ is a bijection, with inverse left translation by $g^{-1}$. Equivariance gives $f(gs)=gf(s)$ for every arrow, so these maps define $\Phi(g)\in\operatorname{Aut}(\omega_G)$. The identities $g(hs)=(gh)s$ and $1s=s$ give a group homomorphism $\Phi$. The pointwise topology on these natural automorphisms is a group topology: to keep $(\alpha\beta)(x)=\alpha(\beta(x))$ fixed it suffices to keep $\beta(x)$ and $\alpha(\beta(x))$ fixed at the given pair; to keep $\alpha^{-1}(x)=y$ fixed it suffices to require $\alpha(y)=x$. Finite intersections give continuity of multiplication and inversion.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5, printed p. 64; elementary orbit-coordinate expansion of its coset-filter argument.

proof.text: For $x=aU\in G/U$, its stabilizer is $aUa^{-1}$, an open subgroup since conjugation is a homeomorphism. Each fibre of $g\mapsto gx$ is a left coset of this subgroup; it is open and closed, because the complementary cosets are open too. Thus the inverse image under $\Phi$ of a basic pointwise-open set is open. If $\Phi(g)=1$, then $gU=U$ for every open $U$, so $g\in\bigcap_U U=\{1\}$: Hausdorffness provides, for any $g\ne1$, an identity neighborhood missing $g$, and the subgroup basis refines it. Moreover $\Phi^{-1}(\{\alpha:\alpha_U(U)=U\})=U$. These last open subgroups form an identity basis of $G$, so once $\Phi$ is bijective its inverse is continuous at the identity, hence everywhere by translation.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5, printed p. 64; elementary orbit-coordinate expansion of its coset-filter argument.

proof.text: Fix $\alpha\in\operatorname{Aut}(\omega_G)$. Given finitely many coordinates $x_j=a_jU_j$, set $V=\bigcap_j a_jU_ja_j^{-1}$, with $V=G$ for the empty list. The formula $q_j(hV)=ha_jU_j$ is well-defined because $V\subseteq a_jU_ja_j^{-1}$ and is equivariant. Choose a representative $b\in G$ of the coset $\alpha_V(V)$. Naturality gives $\alpha_{U_j}(x_j)=q_j(\alpha_V(V))=bx_j$ for every $j$. Thus a single group element realizes any finite list of coordinates of $\alpha$; for the empty list one may use $1$.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5, printed p. 64; elementary orbit-coordinate expansion of its coset-filter argument.

proof.text: Let $D=\coprod_{U\text{ open}}G/U$, a set of tagged coordinates. Direct its finite subsets by inclusion. For each finite $F\subseteq D$ choose $g_F\in G$ realizing $\alpha(x)$ at every $x\in F$, using the preceding step. For each coordinate $x$, the net $(g_Fx)_F$ is eventually constant with value $\alpha(x)$. Also put $C_x=\{g\in G:gx=\alpha(x)\}$. Each $C_x$ is a closed coset by step 3, and step 4 says every finite intersection of the $C_x$ is nonempty, including the empty intersection.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5, printed p. 64; elementary orbit-coordinate expansion of its coset-filter argument.

proof.text: For an open subgroup $U$, let $x=U\in G/U$ and $y=\alpha_U^{-1}(x)$. Once $F,F\prime$ both contain the two tagged coordinates $x,y$, we have $g_Fx=\alpha_U(x)=g_{F\prime}x$ and $g_Fy=x=g_{F\prime}y$. The first equality gives $g_F^{-1}g_{F\prime}\in U$. The second gives $g_F^{-1}x=y=g_{F\prime}^{-1}x$, hence $g_Fg_{F\prime}^{-1}\in U$. Since the open subgroups refine all identity neighborhoods, this is exactly the two-sided Cauchy condition in the hypothesis. Both $\alpha$ and its inverse are essential here; no normality of $U$ is assumed.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5, printed p. 64; elementary orbit-coordinate expansion of its coset-filter argument.

proof.text: If the completeness alternative holds, the Cauchy net just constructed converges to some $g\in G$ by the stated assumption. For each coordinate $x$, its tail lies in $C_x$. As $C_x$ is closed, $g\in C_x$: otherwise its open complement would be a neighborhood of the limit eventually containing the net, a contradiction. Consequently $gx=\alpha(x)$ at every coordinate.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5, printed p. 64; elementary orbit-coordinate expansion of its coset-filter argument.

proof.text: If the compact alternative holds, apply [lem-sfb-compact-closed-finite-intersection] to $X=G$, $I=D$ and the closed sets $C_x$ of step 5. The hypothesis about every open cover having a finite subcover is exactly compactness of $G$, and the finite-intersection hypothesis, including the empty family, is step 4. We obtain $g\in\bigcap_{x\in D}C_x$, so again $gx=\alpha(x)$ at every coordinate.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5 and Example 7.1.6, printed p. 64; compact case via Stacks 005D (lemma-intersection-closed-in-quasi-compact).

proof.text: Under either alternative we have $\Phi(g)_U(x)=\alpha_U(x)$ for every $U$ and every $x\in G/U$. Equality of functions and then of natural transformations gives $\Phi(g)=\alpha$. Thus $\Phi$ is surjective and, by step 3, injective. Its multiplication law is step 2 and both directions are continuous by step 3. This proves the asserted topological group isomorphism for the orbit category.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5, printed p. 64; elementary orbit-coordinate expansion of its coset-filter argument.

proof.text: Let $F_G$ be the underlying-set functor on all discrete continuous left $G$-sets. For any such set $S$ and $s\in S$, its stabilizer $U_s$ is open, since it is the inverse image of the open singleton $\{s\}$ under $g\mapsto gs$. The map $q_s:G/U_s\to S$, $hU_s\mapsto hs$, is well-defined and equivariant. If $\beta\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_G)$ restricts to $\alpha$ on the orbit category, step 9 gives a unique $g$ with $\alpha=\Phi(g)$. Naturality for $q_s$ gives $\beta_S(s)=q_s(\alpha_{U_s}(U_s))=gs$. Conversely the family of translations by any $g$ is natural on all equivariant maps. Hence restriction is bijective, with inverse given by these translation families; it respects multiplication.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5, printed p. 64, sentence that every discrete G-set is a disjoint union of G/U; expanded pointwise without choosing orbit representatives.

proof.text: Restriction is continuous because every orbit-coordinate evaluation is among the evaluations on all discrete actions. For the inverse restriction map, consider a coordinate $s\in S$ and its equivariant map $q_s$ above. For every $\alpha$, its extension satisfies $\beta_S(s)=q_s(\alpha_{U_s}(U_s))$. Evaluation at $U_s$ is continuous by the pointwise topology, and $q_s$ is continuous between discrete sets. Thus this coordinate of the extension is continuous. A basic open condition specifies only finitely many coordinates, so its inverse image is open. This proves that restriction and its inverse preserve the stated topologies.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5, printed p. 64, orbit determination and compact-open (= pointwise on discrete sets) topology.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 7.1.5 and Example 7.1.6, printed pp. 63–64. Explicit finite-coordinate net version of the source coset-filter argument; compact case uses Stacks 005D.
